title: Samsung Cuts Hundreds of US Jobs as It Abandons New Jersey for Texas Headquarters
excerpt: The South Korean tech giant is relocating its U.S. consumer electronics headquarters less than a year after opening new offices in Englewood Cliffs, affecting 739 workers in New Jersey and about 100 more in Texas.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Samsung is cutting 739 jobs in New Jersey and 100 in Texas as it relocates headquarters.
  • The layoffs impact consumer electronics divisions, not the profitable semiconductor unit.
  • Most New Jersey employees received relocation offers, but some were let go, including executives.
  • The move follows the grand opening of the Englewood Cliffs campus less than a year ago.
  • Corporate relocations to Texas raise concerns about New Jersey's business climate.

  • Samsung Electronics America is cutting 739 roles at its Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, headquarters and roughly 100 more at its Plano, Texas, office as it relocates its U.S. consumer electronics headquarters to Texas.
  • The restructuring affects Samsung's display, phone and other consumer electronics divisions — not its booming semiconductor unit, which just posted record profits.
  • Most New Jersey employees have received relocation offers, but an unknown number have been let go, including senior sales and marketing executives.
  • The move comes less than a year after Samsung celebrated the grand opening of its new Englewood Cliffs campus in September 2025.

Samsung Electronics has cut hundreds of jobs at its U.S. consumer electronics operations and is relocating its American headquarters from New Jersey to Texas, according to internal documents and people familiar with the matter, in a move that underscores deepening fault lines inside the South Korean tech giant.

The company confirmed to Reuters on Sunday that 739 roles at its Englewood Cliffs, New Jersey, campus have been affected by the headquarters shift. A majority of those employees received relocation offers to move to Samsung Electronics America's existing campus in Plano, Texas, though others were let go outright.

A Stunning Reversal

The restructuring is striking for its speed. Samsung employees in New Jersey only moved into their new Englewood Cliffs offices with much fanfare in September 2025, an event attended by U.S. Representative Josh Gottheimer and local officials who hailed the investment as a sign of Samsung's commitment to the state. Samsung Electronics America employed about 1,200 workers at the campus, according to a press release from Gottheimer's office at the time.

Less than a year later, those same workers face a stark choice: follow the company to Texas or lose their positions.

"Its semiconductor business has surged to record profitability, driven by demand for high-bandwidth memory chips used in AI data centers."

At Samsung's Plano office, about 100 additional workers — including staff in the company's mobile division — have also been laid off, according to one person who said they were among those affected. Internal documents reviewed by Reuters show the unit notified employees on June 30 of an "enterprise-wide reduction-in-force," describing the impact as involving a "significant number" of positions.

"Samsung Electronics America Inc. is undergoing a business transformation designed to better position our organization for long-term growth and future success."

— Samsung spokesperson

Two Samsungs: Chips Soar, Consumer Electronics Struggles

The layoffs highlight a widening gap between Samsung's divisions. Its semiconductor business has surged to record profitability, driven by demand for high-bandwidth memory chips used in AI data centers. But the consumer electronics arm — responsible for phones, televisions and home appliances — has been under pressure as component costs rise and competition intensifies from Chinese rivals.

Samsung Electronics America, or SEA, oversees the consumer electronics side of the business in the U.S. and is separate from Samsung's chip operations, which are centered around fabrication facilities in Austin and Taylor, Texas. The state has invested heavily in semiconductor manufacturing, including a $250 million grant to Samsung's Taylor facility through the Texas Semiconductor Innovation Fund.

The headquarters move consolidates Samsung's U.S. presence in Texas, where it has maintained operations for more than 30 years. Plano has become a magnet for corporate relocations, with AT&T, Sally Beauty Holdings, KFC and Tech Mahindra all moving headquarters to the Dallas-area suburb in recent months.

What It Means for Indian Professionals

Samsung's U.S. operations employ a significant number of Indian-origin engineers and professionals, particularly in its semiconductor and mobile divisions. The consumer electronics cuts in New Jersey and Texas could affect H-1B visa holders, who face a 60-day grace period to find new employment or transfer their status after a layoff.

The broader trend of corporate relocations from high-cost Northeast states to Texas has implications for the Indian diaspora, which has large, established communities in the New Jersey tri-state area. Workers who accept relocation offers will need to uproot families, while those let go join a competitive job market that has already absorbed more than 150,000 tech layoffs in 2026.

What's Next

Corporate Relocations to Texas
›Texas has become a hub for corporate relocations.
›Recent moves include AT&T and KFC.
›New Jersey faces challenges in retaining businesses.

Samsung said the transition to Plano will be completed by the end of 2026. More than 30 employees, including senior sales and marketing executives from offices in Texas, New Jersey and elsewhere, have recently left the company, according to documents reviewed by Reuters. The full extent of the layoffs across all of Samsung's U.S. operations remains unclear.

New Jersey officials have expressed concern about the departure's impact on the state's business climate. The move adds to a string of corporate exits from the Garden State, raising questions about whether tax policy and cost structures are pushing companies toward more business-friendly jurisdictions.
